title: IPv4 addressing and subnetting
subtitle: An IP address is a 32-bit number cut into “which network” and “which host”. Every subnetting question is where to cut.

addr.title: Reading an address
addr.body: An IPv4 address is 32 bits written as four decimal bytes. The subnet mask (or prefix length /n) marks the first n bits as the network part; the rest identify the host. Originally the split was fixed by class: A (first bit 0, /8), B (10, /16), C (110, /24), D (1110, multicast), E (reserved). Modern CIDR allows any prefix length.

subnet.title: Network, broadcast and usable hosts
subnet.body: AND the address with the mask to get the network address; set all host bits to 1 for the broadcast address; the usable hosts lie between them: 2h − 2 where h is the number of host bits (the all-zeros and all-ones addresses are reserved).
subnet.steps: 192.168.10.77/26: the last byte 77 = 01001101, and /26 leaves 6 host bits. Network: zero the host bits → 01000000 = 64. Broadcast: set them → 01111111 = 127. Usable hosts.

vlsm.title: VLSM: sizing each subnet
vlsm.body: VLSM gives each network just the block it needs. Sort requirements largest first, give each the smallest power-of-two block that fits its hosts + 2, and place blocks back to back so they stay aligned. From 192.168.1.0/24 for 100, 50, 20 and 10 hosts: 192.168.1.0/25 192.168.1.128/26 192.168.1.192/27 192.168.1.224/28.

special.title: Private, public, NAT and multicast
special.body: Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are not routed on the Internet; NAT rewrites a private source address and port to the router’s public address, keeping a table so replies return to the right host. Unicast goes to one host, broadcast to all hosts on a network, multicast (224/4) to a group. IPv6 (128-bit, written in hex) removes the address shortage and most need for NAT; transition uses dual stack, tunnelling or translation.

magic.title: Subnetting by the “magic number”
magic.body: For a mask whose interesting byte is m, the block size ("magic number") is 256 − m. Subnets start at multiples of it. For /26 the mask byte is 192, the block size 64, so subnets start at 0, 64, 128, 192 — and 77 falls in the block starting at 64.
magic.steps: Which subnet holds 10.1.1.130/27? /27 → mask byte 224 → block 32. Multiples of 32: …, 96, 128, 160. 130 lies in the block starting at 128. So network 10.1.1.128, broadcast 10.1.1.159, usable .129–.158.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Network = address AND mask; broadcast = host bits all 1; hosts = 2ʰ − 2.
  • VLSM: largest block first.
  • NAT trades address space for a translation table.
